text: A dashboard is the layer that sits above both reports and PA widgets, and the single most important thing to understand about it is that it's a container, not a chart of its own.

Report Designer builds one report at a time. Performance Analytics builds one indicator and its widget. A dashboard is a page that holds many of those side by side, organized onto one or more tabs, so a manager can see everything at once instead of opening six separate reports. The dashboard itself generates no new data — it's purely a canvas that arranges content that already exists.

That means the order of operations matters. You build the report — the Pie chart, the Bar chart — in Report Designer first, using everything from Lesson 28. You build any PA indicator and widget separately, using Lesson 29. Only after those exist do you open ServiceNow's Dashboard application, start a new dashboard, and use Add Content to select the already-built report or widget by name and place it on the canvas.

Three settings are what turn a populated dashboard into a genuinely usable one. Size and layout let you resize and reposition each widget on the canvas grid, so the most important chart gets the most visual weight. Refresh interval controls how often widgets automatically re-pull data, which matters most for a live operational dashboard meant to stay open on a wall monitor all day. And role-based visibility restricts who can even open the dashboard in the first place — a setting that deserves the same up-front attention as a report's filter condition, not a fix applied after the fact.

Report, then widget, then dashboard, then visibility — that's the real build order, and skipping any one of those steps out of sequence is the most common way a new admin ends up with a dashboard that's hard to maintain. Next, the reporting lab: a full worked scenario that walks through all of it end to end, from a plain-language request to a finished, role-restricted dashboard.
